cases.subject: C++
cases.question: How do constructors and destructors work in C++?
expected_facts: Explain creation/initialization by constructors and destruction/cleanup by destructors.
cases.answer:
A default constructor is a member function requiring no parameters when called, named after the type it constructs, and is used to initialize objects. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 240]

A destructor is a function without arguments, named after the type with a tilde prefix, that is called when a user-defined object is about to be destroyed in order to clean up resources like dynamically allocated memory. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 242]

Constructors run when an object is created to set up its state, such as locking a mutex or initializing members, while destructors run automatically when an object is destroyed to perform cleanup tasks like unlocking a mutex. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 240] [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 242] [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 469]
cases.review_note: Reviewed the main requested fact(s) against the supplied/cited book text.

cases.subject: C
cases.question: How do malloc and free manage dynamically allocated memory in C?
expected_facts: malloc obtains dynamic storage; free releases it.
cases.answer:
The standard C library provides functions including malloc() and free() defined in the <stdlib.h> header for managing dynamically allocated memory. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 267]

The malloc() function requests a specified total size of memory in bytes and returns the starting address of the newly created memory chunk as a pointer. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 267]

Because malloc() might fail to service a request, it can return a null pointer, which should be checked to prevent dereferencing. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 267]

The free() function is used to release memory that was dynamically allocated when it is no longer needed. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 267] [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 268]

After calling free() on a pointer, using its value results in undefined behavior until a new value is stored in it. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 268]
cases.review_note: Reviewed the main requested fact(s) against the supplied/cited book text.

These methods return the converted strings as new String instances because String is immutable in Java. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 77]

cases.subject: Python
cases.question: What is the difference between lists and tuples in Python?
expected_facts: Lists are mutable and tuples immutable; avoid claiming contained mutable values cannot change.
cases.answer:
Lists are enclosed in brackets, whereas tuples are enclosed in parentheses. [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 59]

List elements and size can be changed, while tuples are immutable, fixed-length, and cannot be updated, meaning their items cannot be added, modified, or removed once initialized. [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 59] [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 186] [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 42]

Tuples do not have append and extend methods like lists do. [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 186]
cases.review_note: Mutability contrast is supported; parentheses wording repeats introductory shorthand despite the comma distinction in PDF p.185.

cases.subject: C++
cases.question: What is a default constructor in C++?
expected_facts: A default constructor can be called without arguments; default arguments can satisfy this.
cases.answer:
A default constructor is a type of constructor that requires no parameters when called. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 240]

It is a member function named after the type it constructs. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 240]

The compiler implicitly provides an empty default constructor when certain conditions are met. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 240]
cases.review_note: The definition can omit the nuance of constructors whose parameters all have default arguments.

cases.subject: C
cases.question: What is the difference between malloc and calloc in C?
expected_facts: calloc zero-initializes allocated storage; malloc does not initialize it.
cases.answer:
malloc and calloc are functions provided by the standard C library for dynamic memory allocation. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 267]

malloc takes the total size of the memory in bytes, whereas calloc takes the number of elements and the size of each element. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 267]

calloc initializes all bits of the allocated memory to zero. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 268]

Most implementations optimize calloc for performance making it faster than calling malloc followed by memset, even though the net effect is identical. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 268]
cases.review_note: calloc zero-initialization is explicit; the answer does not explicitly contrast malloc leaving storage uninitialized.

cases.subject: Java
cases.question: Must equal Java objects have equal hashCode values, and can unequal objects share a hash code?
expected_facts: Equal objects require equal hash codes; unequal objects may collide.
cases.answer:
If two objects are equal according to the equals method, calling hashCode on each object must produce the same integer result. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 253] [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 257]

It is not required for unequal objects to produce distinct integer hash code results, meaning unequal objects can share a hash code. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 253]

cases.subject: Python
cases.question: How does dict.get return a default value for a missing key?
expected_facts: dict.get returns a supplied default, or None, when a key is absent.
cases.answer:
The dict.get method allows you to return a default value if a key is not found, avoiding the KeyError exception that occurs with square bracket lookups. [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 555] [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 137] [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 134]

By default, if the key does not exist, dict.get returns None, but you can pass a second value to return instead during a failed lookup. [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 137] [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 134]

cases.subject: C++
cases.question: When is a destructor called in C++?
expected_facts: Called when the object is destroyed; examples include scope exit or deletion.
cases.answer:
A destructor is called when a user-defined object is about to be destroyed. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 242]

Automatic variables are destroyed when they go out of scope. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 242]

Using the delete operator on a pointer to an object or array calls its destructor. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 242]

cases.subject: Python
cases.question: How does a with statement close a file in Python?
expected_facts: The with/context-manager pattern closes the file on leaving its block, including exceptions.
cases.answer:
The with statement acts as a context manager that allows you to indent code under an open file, providing a more elegant and explicit way to ensure the file is closed. [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 549]

The with statement always closes a file automatically after the indented block finishes, even if an exception is raised. [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 549]

cases.subject: C++
cases.question: How do virtual function calls behave in constructors and destructors?
expected_facts: During construction/destruction, virtual dispatch must be explained for the class currently being constructed/destroyed rather than as a general constructor definition.
cases.answer:
During the construction and destruction of objects, the dynamic type of the object is treated as the class of the current constructor or destructor rather than a more-derived class. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 235]

When a virtual function is called from a base class constructor or destructor, the base class version of the function is called. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 235]

When a virtual function is called from a derived class constructor or destructor, the derived class version of the function is called. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 235]

This behavior prevents unsafe calls to member functions that might rely on derived members which are either not yet initialized during construction or already destroyed during destruction. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 235]
cases.review_note: Reviewed the main requested fact(s) against the supplied/cited book text.

cases.subject: C++
cases.question: Why should a C++ base class have a virtual destructor when deleting a derived object through a base pointer?
expected_facts: A virtual base destructor enables correct derived destruction; deleting this way without one can be undefined behavior.
cases.answer:
Deleting a derived object through a base pointer whose static type lacks a virtual destructor results in undefined behavior if the static and dynamic types are different. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 541]

A virtual destructor in a base class causes object destruction to check the vtable, automatically calling the correct destructor based on the dynamic type. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 149]

cases.subject: C
cases.question: Are function arguments passed by value in C?
expected_facts: Arguments are passed by value, including copied pointer values.
cases.answer:
In C, all function parameters are passed by value. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 161]

Modifying a parameter in a callee function does not affect the caller function's local variables because of pass by value. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 161]

Pointers can be used to let callee functions modify caller functions' local variables by passing the pointer values pointing at the local variables rather than using pass by reference. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 161]

cases.subject: All
cases.question: How do constructors and destructors work in C++?
expected_facts: Explain creation/initialization by constructors and destruction/cleanup by destructors.
cases.answer:
A default constructor is a member function that requires no parameters when called, is named after the type it constructs, and can use a member initializer list and constructor function body to initialize members. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 240]

A destructor is a function without arguments, named after its type with a tilde prefix, that is called when a user-defined object is about to be destroyed to clean up resources such as deleting dynamically allocated arrays. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 242]

When an object of a derived class is destructed, it calls its own destructor followed by the destructors of its members and its base class. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 242]

Constructors and destructors can manage resource lifecycles automatically, such as a constructor locking a mutex and its destructor guaranteeing the unlock is called when exiting a scope. [C++ Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 469]

cases.subject: All
cases.question: How do malloc and free manage dynamically allocated memory in C?
expected_facts: malloc obtains dynamic storage; free releases it.
cases.answer:
For managing dynamically allocated memory, the standard C library provides functions including malloc() and free(), which are defined in the <stdlib.h> header. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 267]

The malloc() function requests a specified number of bytes from memory and assigns the starting address of the newly created memory chunk to a pointer. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 267]

Because malloc might fail to service a request, it may return a null pointer, which should be checked to prevent later attempts to dereference it. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 267]

Memory dynamically allocated using malloc() can be released when no longer needed by calling the free() function. [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 267] [C Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 268]

cases.answer:
Lists are enclosed in brackets and their elements and size can be changed, while tuples are enclosed in parentheses and cannot be updated. [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 59]

Tuples are immutable, which means one cannot add, modify, or remove items once the tuple is initialized. [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 186] [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 42]

Tuples do not have .append and .extend methods as lists do. [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 186]

A tuple is fixed-length, whereas a list's size can be changed. [Python Notes for Professionals, PDF p. 42]
